summary: The narrator, a documentary director working on a picture about single women adopting children, arranges to shoot a second interview with Paula Marks, a 43-year-old children's book writer in her prewar West Side apartment. Crew members handle the cramped space, makeup is negotiated with Paula, and her toddler adopted daughter Rachel interrupts the shoot. Paula's account of the adoption process closely mirrors Carly Grove's, including the difficulties described by NYSAC, New York Singles Adopting Children. The narrator is under budget and time pressure to produce a rough cut and sell the film to cable in six weeks.
one_line: A director shoots a second single-mother adoption interview with children's author Paula Marks, whose account echoes Carly Grove's.
key_facts: The director needed to produce a rough cut and sell the picture to cable in six weeks because money was going fast.
The executive producer, David, normally would have had access to the director's picture under the standard director's contract, but the narrator believed that prerogative was now out the window.
The narrator deeply needed at least one more interview because Carly Grove's interview was too much of a happy one-note.
Paula Marks was forty-three, tall and willowy, had let her hair start going to gray, and had pale brown eyes.
Paula Marks wrote children's books, had never married, and decided to adopt a child because she had a lot of extra love she felt was going to waste.
The shoot with Paula Marks took place on Thursday and the appointment had taken all weekend, including a Sunday brunch, to set up.
Paula's apartment was in a sprawling prewar West Side building with thick plaster walls and a rabbit's warren of halls and foyers.
Paula initially insisted she did not want makeup because she never wore it and did not want to appear on camera looking like Barbie.
Arlene persuaded Paula that cameras lie and the only way to look like yourself is to enhance the qualities that make you you.
Paula's adopted daughter Rachel was a year and a half old and dragged a doll she named Angie, which came out as 'Ann-gee'.
Erica, the production manager, taught Rachel how to play patty-cake.
Rachel covered herself head to toe in Ragu tomato sauce within five minutes of eating spaghetti.
Paula's account of the adoption process was almost identical to Carly Grove's story.
Paula had consulted legal services recommended by NYSAC, New York Singles Adopting Children, which described a scenario of delays, paperwork and heartache.
According to NYSAC's legal services, adoption could be done but could take years.
